question: Moving from left to right across a period of the periodic table, what is the general trend in atomic (covalent) radius and first ionization energy?
options: Atomic radius increases and first ionization energy decreases.
Atomic radius decreases and first ionization energy increases.
Atomic radius and first ionization energy both increase.
Atomic radius and first ionization energy both remain unchanged.
gold_answer: Atomic radius decreases and first ionization energy increases.
notes: Question, options and claims are original wording. All evidence passages are verbatim excerpts from OpenStax, Chemistry (1e), section 6.5 Periodic Variations in Element Properties, retrieved 2026-11-19; that book is released under the Creative Commons Attribution licence (CC BY 4.0). Subscripts in mathematical symbols are normalized to plain text. All nine claims draw on this single section; a second independent source is recommended before freezing.

positions.answer: Atomic radius increases and first ionization energy decreases.

claims.text: Moving from left to right across a period, the covalent radius generally decreases.

evidence.text: As shown in Figure 6.32, as we move across a period from left to right, we generally find that each element has a smaller covalent radius than the element preceding it.
evidence.notes: Section 6.5, subsection 'Variation in Covalent Radius'; verbatim.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states that covalent radius generally decreases from left to right across a period, which entails the claim.

claims.text: First ionization energy generally decreases from left to right across a period.

evidence.text: Relating this logic to what we have just learned about radii, we would expect first ionization energies to decrease down a group and to increase across a period.
evidence.notes: Section 6.5, subsection 'Variation in Ionization Energies'; verbatim.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage assigns a decrease to motion down a group and an increase across a period; the claim assigns the decrease to the across-period direction, reversing the stated relation.

claims.text: Moving down a group, the covalent radius increases.

evidence.text: Radius increases as we move down a group, so Ge < Fl (Note: Fl is the symbol for flerovium, element 114, NOT fluorine). Radius decreases as we move across a period, so Kr < Br < Ge.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states directly that radius increases moving down a group, so the claim is entailed.

positions.answer: Atomic radius decreases and first ionization energy increases.

claims.text: As we move across a period from left to right, each element generally has a smaller covalent radius than the element preceding it.

evidence.text: As shown in Figure 6.32, as we move across a period from left to right, we generally find that each element has a smaller covalent radius than the element preceding it.
evidence.notes: Section 6.5, subsection 'Variation in Covalent Radius'; verbatim.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states this exact trend, so it entails the claim.

claims.text: First ionization energies are expected to increase across a period.

evidence.text: Relating this logic to what we have just learned about radii, we would expect first ionization energies to decrease down a group and to increase across a period.
evidence.notes: Section 6.5, subsection 'Variation in Ionization Energies'; verbatim.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage explicitly states the expectation that first ionization energies increase across a period, which entails the claim.

claims.text: The effective nuclear charge increases as we move from left to right across a period.

evidence.text: Thus, Zeff increases as we move from left to right across a period. The stronger pull (higher effective nuclear charge) experienced by electrons on the right side of the periodic table draws them closer to the nucleus, making the covalent radii smaller.
evidence.notes: Section 6.5, subsection 'Variation in Covalent Radius'; subscript Z_eff normalized to Zeff.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states that effective nuclear charge (Zeff) increases from left to right across a period, so the claim is entailed.

positions.answer: Atomic radius increases and first ionization energy decreases.

claims.text: The covalent radius generally increases from left to right across a period.

evidence.text: As shown in Figure 6.32, as we move across a period from left to right, we generally find that each element has a smaller covalent radius than the element preceding it.
evidence.notes: Section 6.5, subsection 'Variation in Covalent Radius'; verbatim.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states that covalent radius generally decreases across a period, the opposite direction to the claim.

claims.text: Elements in the same group have similar chemical behavior because they have the same number and distribution of electrons in their valence shells.

evidence.text: The elements in groups (vertical columns) of the periodic table exhibit similar chemical behavior. This similarity occurs because the members of a group have the same number and distribution of electrons in their valence shells.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states both the similar behavior of group members and its valence-electron cause, so the claim is entailed.

claims.text: Elements within a group have identical covalent radii.

evidence.text: The elements in groups (vertical columns) of the periodic table exhibit similar chemical behavior. This similarity occurs because the members of a group have the same number and distribution of electrons in their valence shells.

claims.verdict_rationale: The cited passage describes similar chemical behavior and valence-electron configuration within a group but says nothing about covalent radii being identical, so it neither establishes nor refutes the claim.
